question: What is another name for the body's specific defense system?
explanation: We call them specific defences the adaptive immune system because they adapt and target exact germs over time. You've got this! [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why is immune tolerance so important for the body?

options.A: It prevents the immune system from attacking healthy body tissues.
options.B: It stops foreign bacteria from multiplying inside the digestive tract.
options.C: It helps the body produce more white blood cells during a fever.
options.D: It allows white blood cells to travel quickly through the bloodstream.

explanation: Immune tolerance is like a safety switch that ensures your white blood cells don't mistakenly destroy your own healthy cells. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h1)

question: What exactly is an epitope?

options.A: A chemical substance released by damaged skin tissue
options.B: The specific part of an antigen that immune receptors bind to
options.C: A large white blood cell found inside the lymph nodes
options.D: The protective protein coat surrounding a harmful virus

explanation: Think of an epitope as the specific handle or tag on a germ that immune cells grab onto. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h2)

question: What makes an immunogen different from a regular antigen?

options.A: All immunogens trigger a response, but not all antigens do so on their own.
options.B: Antigens are made of proteins, while immunogens are always made of lipids.
options.C: Immunogens are harmless to humans, whereas antigens are always toxic.
options.D: Antigens only attack the skin, while immunogens attack internal organs.

explanation: All immunogens are antigens, but immunogens are the ones that successfully provoke a full-blown immune fight! [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h2)

question: Where do T-lymphocytes go to mature?
explanation: T-cells are born in the bone marrow, but they travel to the thymus gland to grow up and finish their training. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h3)

question: What is the main job of secondary lymphoid organs like lymph nodes?

options.A: They produce brand new stem cells that turn into red blood cells.
options.B: They filter out waste products and excess water from the urinary tract.
options.C: They trap pathogens and provide a meeting place for mature immune cells.
options.D: They manufacture the primary hormones needed to regulate body temperature.

explanation: Lymph nodes act like checkpoint stations where immune cells hang out and catch invading germs. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which cells turn into antibody-producing factories during humoral immunity?
explanation: When B-cells get activated, they transform into plasma cells whose full-time job is pumping out antibodies. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why does a repeat infection with the same virus trigger a much faster immune response?

options.A: Memory B-cells formed during the first infection quickly recognize the virus.
options.B: Red blood cells absorb the viral toxins before they reach the lymph nodes.
options.C: Innate white blood cells stop destroying friendly bacteria in the gut.
options.D: The body's skin barriers become thicker to prevent the virus from entering.

explanation: Memory B-cells remember past battles, letting your body skip the slow setup phase and fight back instantly. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h4)

question: What is the main task of cytotoxic T-cells?

options.A: Producing free-floating antibodies in the blood plasma
options.B: Destroying infected or cancerous body cells directly
options.C: Filtering waste materials out of the lymphatic fluid
options.D: Producing new red blood cells inside the bone marrow

explanation: Cytotoxic T-cells are the body's direct hit squad—they spot infected or abnormal cells and destroy them. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why are helper T-cells considered the master coordinators of the immune system?

options.A: They physically swallow large bacteria and digest them inside stomach acid.
options.B: They create a hard physical barrier around damaged skin to stop bleeding.
options.C: They release chemical signals that activate both B-cells and other T-cells.
options.D: They turn into red blood cells when the body suffers from severe anemia.

explanation: Helper T-cells act like military commanders, sending chemical messages to rally both B-cells and other T-cells into action. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which part of an antibody molecule binds directly to a specific antigen?
explanation: The tips of the Y-shaped antibody have a variable region that fits onto antigens like a lock and key. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h6)

question: What happens during opsonization?

options.A: Viruses are blocked from entering healthy cells by sticky chemical covers.
options.B: Blood vessels widen to allow white blood cells to reach an infected tissue.
options.C: Proteins form large holes in the outer cell wall of invading bacteria.
options.D: Antibodies coat a pathogen so phagocytic cells can easily recognize and swallow it.

explanation: Opsonization is like putting a glowing tag on a germ so phagocytes can spot it and gobble it up easily. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is a major characteristic of passive immunity?

options.A: It stimulates the bone marrow to produce permanent memory cells.
options.B: It only occurs after a patient recovers from a severe viral illness.
options.C: It provides immediate protection that fades relatively quickly.
options.D: It requires the body several weeks to manufacture its own T-cells.

explanation: Passive immunity gives you ready-made antibodies right away, but it wears off because your body didn't make memory cells. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h7)

question: An infant receives protective antibodies through breast milk. What type of immunity is this?
explanation: This is natural passive immunity because the mother's antibodies pass naturally to the baby to give temporary protection. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is the main goal of giving someone a vaccine?

options.A: To provide temporary ready-made antibodies that last for one week
options.B: To physically block viruses from entering the body through the skin
options.C: To destroy all normal bacteria living inside the gastrointestinal tract
options.D: To stimulate memory cell production without causing severe disease

explanation: Vaccines introduce safe pieces of a germ so your immune system can build memory cells without you getting sick. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h8)

question: How does a secondary immune response compare to a primary immune response?

options.A: It produces only short-lived antibodies that cannot destroy viruses.
options.B: It relies entirely on innate barriers rather than white blood cells.
options.C: It causes severe clinical illness because the pathogen is stronger.
options.D: It is faster and produces a much larger amount of antibodies.

explanation: Because of memory cells, the secondary response acts fast and floods your system with antibodies to stop infections early. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h8)
